Pursue clean code that works, delivered now, as the goal of every change.
Write production code only in response to a currently failing automated test, and continuously eliminate duplication; these are the two core rules of TDD.
Recognize TDD's limits: do not rely on tests alone for software whose goals need human judgment or cannot be reliably reproduced, such as security and subtle concurrency.

Do not implement all tests at once; instead, in pure TDD stay never more than one change from green, writing newly-implied tests and refactorings onto the list and handling every leftover item at session end while never deferring a test you suspect might fail.

When adopting TDD on a legacy codebase, do not test and refactor the whole system at once; limit the scope of changes, leave working-but-ugly parts alone, and break the test/refactoring deadlock with other feedback such as a careful partner and imperfect system-level tests.

Follow the red-green-refactor cycle: write a small failing test, make it pass as quickly as possible even with expedient code, then remove all introduced duplication; run all tests after each small change.
Treat a red bar as concrete progress; in the green phase aim only to pass the test, then generalize a limited implementation before moving to the next test.
Make it work first and make it clean second; quick green excuses expedient code only until the refactor step completes.
Allow copy-and-edit to reach green quickly only if the duplication is removed before the next test.
Force a real change by choosing test parameters that break the current implementation, reaching green with localized ugly code and then moving it where it belongs once tests pass.
Run the tests between every refactoring step to confirm behavior is unchanged.

Integrate at each passing test with duplication removed to shorten CI cycles to roughly 15 to 30 minutes, achieving simple design by coding only what the tests need and removing all duplication, while a growing test suite lets you attempt more aggressive large-scale refactorings.
Work in small increments with each test covering a tiny slice of functionality, taking smaller steps the harder the problem while retaining the ability to take larger steps.
When a test is too big to implement in one step, invent a smaller test that represents real progress toward it.
Use TDD to manage programming fear by shortening the gap between decision and feedback.
Treat TDD as a steering process with no single right step size: bigger steps when confident, smaller steps when unsure.
Treat mastery of TDD as being able to take tiny steps when the situation calls for them, not always taking them.

Design for testability: compose the system from many highly cohesive, loosely coupled components, demand a development environment with rapid response, and grow the design organically from running-code feedback.

When building a testing framework, focus on supporting a set of isolated, composable test cases rather than on implementation details, and distinguish assertion failures from other errors because failures take longer to debug.

Keep tests fully isolated: they must not affect one another, must be fast enough to run yourself often, and should be sought at a smaller scale than the whole application, which forces a highly cohesive, loosely coupled design.
Have developers write their own tests rather than waiting for someone else.
Maintain a written to-do list of tests, marking items in progress, crossing them off when done, and adding new tests as they occur.
Start from the simplest failing test, imagining the ideal interface and working backward from that API.
Before using an unfamiliar external library facility, write a Learning Test that verifies the API behaves as expected, and re-run those tests when new releases arrive.
Get to green minimally by doing the least to compile and fixing one error at a time, and seek a concrete numerical measure of progress.
When a desired test cannot go green quickly, back off to a more specific achievable test, get to green, then generalize.
Attack dependency by removing its symptom, duplication — including duplication between test data and code — before writing the next test, so the next test passes with a single change.
Isolate a change by adding a parameter in the test so the implementation can change without affecting the test, and vice versa.
Apply Value Object discipline: keep values immutable after construction, return a new object from every operation, and implement equals (and hashCode when used as a hash key) to avoid aliasing bugs.
Compare an object's meaningful attributes, not its concrete class, when implementing equality.

Design a Value Object by setting state at creation and never changing it, returning a new object from every operation and implementing equality (and usually hashing), to defeat the aliasing problem; address allocation performance only with realistic data, usage, profiling, and actual complaints.
Reducing defect density far enough can shift quality assurance from reactive to proactive work.
Translate a design objection or aesthetic discomfort into a concrete failing test case.

Choose a get-to-green strategy deliberately — Fake It (return a constant, then replace with variables), Obvious Implementation (type the real code when confident and quick), or Triangulation (generalize only with two or more examples) — and downshift to Fake It on an unexpected red bar, reserving Triangulation for when you are unsure how to refactor.

Reach green with Fake It (return a constant, then transform into a real expression), since having something green is better than nothing and a green bar gives certainty and scope control by letting you generalize from one concrete example.

Drive abstraction conservatively with Triangulation once two or more examples demand it, reserving it for when you are very unsure of the abstraction and otherwise typing the Obvious Implementation while downshifting to smaller steps when red bars surprise you.
Defer operations that are not needed yet to the to-do list instead of implementing them now.
Tighten visibility as soon as the tests allow, for example making an instance variable private once direct comparison removes the need for outside access.
Express each behavior as both code and test to reduce defects, but do not assume this guarantees correctness and do not strive for perfection — learn the missing test and move on.

Eliminate duplication structurally: introduce factory methods to decouple clients from concrete subclasses, reconcile near-duplicate methods to a common supertype, and push identical members up into a superclass.
Replace explicit class checks with polymorphism, promoting a shared method onto a common interface so dispatch eliminates casts and class checks.
Before deleting a test, keep it if it still exercises unique logic and treat a fully redundant test as a deletion candidate.
Do not mark a test done until the duplication it introduced has been eliminated.
Keep a redundant test if removing it would reduce confidence or if it communicates a distinct scenario, deleting the less useful one only when it is redundant on both confidence and communication.
Protect the refactoring rhythm: entertain only a brief interruption and never interrupt an interruption, and when a larger step goes wrong, unwind it, shift to smaller steps, and redo.
Reduce repeatable behavior to explicit rules so applying them becomes rote and fast, freeing time and energy for creativity when a genuine exception arises.

Focus on one mode at a time: while adding functionality only try to pass a test, and while refactoring only try to get the design right, which yields a 'rapid unhurriedness' where steady one-thing-at-a-time progress turns out to be fast.
Ask the computer instead of reasoning at length about whether a change is safe: make the change and run the tests.
Improve confusing test-failure messages by adding diagnostics such as a toString implementation.

Test rarely-invoked error code deliberately with a Crash Test Dummy that throws instead of doing real work, overriding just the one method needed to keep the test readable, because untested code does not work.

Never change real model code without a supporting test; the conservative response to a red bar is to back out to green, write the test, fix, and reapply — though writing a little code without a test first is acceptable for immediately-visible low-risk output or while already on a red bar, and prefer not to author a new test while red.
Apply YAGNI: do not add a parameter or capability speculatively; add it only when a test demands it.

Verify assumptions pragmatically: write a small test for unfamiliar language or library behavior, allow a refactoring's private helper to rely on existing tests, and use a quick suboptimal implementation to get running before improving it with real usage data.
Follow the compiler, treating compile errors as a focusing to-do list, and when generalizing types change declarations from the leaves back toward the root test to avoid cascading breakage.
Capture a surprising discovery or a refactoring mistake by writing a test that communicates or isolates it.
Separate two intertwined responsibilities so each can be worked on independently, recombining them only if that proves right.
Generalize code that works for one instance to many by replacing constants with variables, relying on TDD's concrete running examples rather than abstract reasoning.
Place operations near the data they act on, moving a method to the class that owns the attributes it uses.
Avoid Pluggable Selector because it makes code hard to analyze statically.

Use a Pluggable Selector to store and dynamically invoke a method name only when cleaning up a straightforward situation of one-method subclasses, mindful that its main drawback is the difficulty of tracing whether a method is invoked.
Structure most tests as Arrange-Act-Assert: create objects, stimulate them, then check results.
Build a clean fixture in setUp() before each test, favoring simplicity of test writing over raw performance, and simplify a test to stop checking something only when another test reliably covers it.
Test that one object communicates correctly with another using Self Shunt, having the object under test talk to the test case itself, which reads better by keeping expected and actual together.

Automate result-checking with specific boolean assertions that remove all human judgment, putting the expected value first in equality assertions and asserting observable behavior rather than implementation details so a test survives a representation change.
Drive a test from a table of input and expected-output values to factor out duplicated assertion structure and make adding cases cheap.

Balance test performance against test isolation, and prevent test coupling — run each test in a fresh instance with freshly created objects so one failure means one problem and tests stay order-independent.
Release external resources in tearDown() so tests stay independent, leaving the world in the same state as before each test.
Record method calls in an ordered log rather than many boolean flags to assert both that methods ran and the order in which they ran.
Assert call order with a string log appended as each message runs, using a set comparison instead when order does not matter.
Recognize that having automated tests is fundamentally different from manually testing, and that automated testing inverts the stress-testing vicious loop into a virtuous cycle.
Implementing xUnit yourself in a new language is a fast way to explore the facilities you will use daily.
Running a new test even when you expect it to fail can surface a mistaken assumption, so it is sometimes worth running.

Before coding, write down a list of all the tests you know you will need — examples of every operation, null or degenerate versions of operations that do not yet exist, and the refactorings needed for clean code — rather than holding it in your head, and never take a step without knowing where your foot will land.
Write the test before the code it tests, using test-first primarily as a design and scope-control tool rather than after-the-fact verification.

Write a test's assertions first and work backward to create the setup they require, building a system from the stories you want to tell, a feature from the tests it should pass, and a test from the asserts that should pass — which separates 'what is the right answer?' and 'how will I check it?' from the other problems.

Choose test data that makes the test easy to read for a future human, making any difference between values meaningful and never using the same constant to mean more than one thing so a reversed-argument bug cannot hide.
Reflect multiple inputs only when the system must handle them, using no more data than is needed to drive the same design decisions.
Prefer Realistic Data over made-up data when testing real-time event traces, doing parallel testing against a prior system, or refactoring a simulation that must produce identical answers.
Pick the next test as one that will teach you something and that you are confident you can implement, growing the program from the known toward the unknown.

Start with a degenerate Starter Test whose output equals its input and whose input is as small as possible, keeping the red-green-refactor loop to minutes by choosing trivially easy inputs and outputs.
Spread TDD by asking for and giving explanations in terms of concrete test cases, never by forcing the practice on people.
When a tangential idea arises during discussion, add a test to the list and return to the topic.
On a defect report, first write the smallest possible failing test that the fix will repair, then ask how you could have known to write it originally.
When you feel lost and the code has become a mess, throw the code away and start over rather than untwisting it; switching pair partners helps motivate productive do-overs.
Allocate hardware and furniture deliberately: invest in the best chairs and the fastest shared development machines, economizing elsewhere.

When a test turns out too big, write a smaller child test for the broken part, get it running, then reintroduce the larger test, first pausing to learn what would have made it smaller; maintaining the rhythm and minimizing time at a red bar is worth extra effort.

Test an object that depends on an expensive or complicated resource with a Mock Object that returns constants, gaining performance, reliability, readability, and lower coupling, while mitigating the risk of divergence with a shared test set run against both mock and real object.
Keep interfaces as narrow as possible, with empty stub implementations returning a reasonable value or throwing depending on whether an unexpected call should be flagged.

End a solo session by leaving the last test broken as a concrete bookmark, but on a team end with all tests passing, always making every test pass before check-in and never commenting out a test to make the suite pass.

When an integration test breaks at check-in, either discard your work and start over or allow a few minutes to fix it before starting over, and run the whole suite all the time until it becomes annoyingly slow.
Implement an operation for a single object first, then extend it to collections (One to Many).

Factor common fixture setup into setUp() when readers cannot easily remember it but keep it inline when top-to-bottom readability matters more, making each distinct fixture its own TestCase subclass created and discarded per use; there is no one-to-one mapping between test and model classes.
Release external resources in tearDown() so each test leaves the world unchanged.

Represent each test case as a method named with a 'test' prefix whose remaining name explains why it exists, keeping test methods short, readable, straight-line code and outlining test categories that become documentation of the class contract.
Test an expected exception by catching exactly that exception and ignoring it, calling fail() if it is not thrown.
Run all tests together by composing a suite of suites, one per package and one aggregating them for the whole application.

Recognize that most programming problems are generated by the tools we use, so internal subproblems recur with common solutions, and treat refactoring as a design activity rather than a separate up-front phase.
Use the Command pattern when a plain message is not enough, representing an invocation as an object seeded with its parameters and triggered through generic protocol such as run().
Use a Null Object to represent a special or base case with the same protocol as regular objects, eliminating repeated null checks.

Use a Template Method written entirely in terms of other methods to express an invariant sequence while allowing subclass refinement, declaring a substep abstract when the computation is meaningless without it, and discovering templates through refactoring rather than up-front design before moving them to the superclass.
Replace a spreading explicit conditional with a Pluggable Object that has two or more implementations, acting the second time you see the conditional.
Use a Factory Method to create an object through a method when you need flexibility to return a different class without changing callers; otherwise plain constructors suffice.

Introduce variation by adding a new implementation of an existing protocol (Imposter) rather than conditional logic, adding an if-statement only when there is one obvious place and no duplicated logic.

Implement a Composite as an Imposter for its components through a shared interface; the real-world conceptual disconnect is usually worth the code simplification, and Composites and Imposters are discovered by eliminating duplication.
Collect results spread across several objects with a Collecting Parameter, a common consequence of Composite introduced as expected results grow more sophisticated.

Do not introduce global variables (Singletons) to languages that lack them; invest the time in better design instead, and never use 'all tests passed' as an excuse to check in code you know is flawed.
In TDD a refactoring preserves the semantics that matter — the currently passing tests — which obliges you to keep enough tests for that equivalence to be trustworthy.
Avoid leap-of-faith refactorings that rely on long chains of reasoning; reduce them with small steps and concrete feedback.
Expect slower test-compile-run-refactor cycles to tempt larger steps and fewer intermediate refactorings; counter this deliberately.

Unify two similar pieces of code by gradually bringing them closer and merging only when absolutely identical, applying this at every scale (loops, conditional branches, methods, classes) and sometimes working backward by making the last step trivial.
Isolate the part that must change before changing it, then consider inlining to undo the isolation, balancing the cost of an extra method against making a concept explicit.
Migrate between data representations by temporarily duplicating the data: add the new format, set and use it everywhere the old one was, then delete the old format.
Use Extract Method to turn part of a long method into a well-named method and Inline Method to collapse twisted control flow or reel yourself back from over-abstraction.
Introduce a second implementation with Extract Interface, naming the interface for the underlying concept rather than prefixing it with 'I'.

Treat more than one message sent to another object within a method as a signal to apply Move Method, which is valuable because the need is visible without deep understanding, its mechanics are quick and safe, and its results are often enlightening.
Turn a complicated method with many parameters and locals into a Method Object so its locals become instance variables and you gain a namespace for further extraction.
Add a parameter by adding it to any interface first, then using compiler errors to find every caller that must change.
Trust that TDD's effectiveness is independent of system size, because eliminating duplication yields many small objects testable in isolation.

Use application-level tests to capture what users actually want, while accepting their fixturing and organizational challenges: establish red-green-refactor in your own practice first, keep programmer-level TDD for immediate green bars and simpler design, and spread the practice afterward.
Treat TDD as encoding a value system that assumes better code leads to more success, so it suits those who revisit and refine their code rather than those who slam code together once.

Value how TDD shortens the design-decision feedback loop to seconds or minutes and behaves like an attractor that converges code toward correctness as features are added one at a time after all tests pass.
Remember that good engineering is only about a fifth of a project's success: bad engineering can sink a project, but modest engineering enables success when the rest lines up.
When implementing a pattern-driven design with TDD, think about what you want the system to do and let the design emerge, because pre-committed design ideas often turn out wrong.
Treat TDD as fundamentally an analysis and design technique for structuring all development, driving development with tests rather than speculation or specifications.
Find and fix defects as early as possible because the cost rises sharply over time, even though TDD's superiority over alternatives is supported by anecdote rather than scientific proof.

Combine TDD with pairing and working fresh: tests are shared conversation pieces, a fresh partner takes over when the rhythm leads you to work tired, and you stop when you cannot get a test, or two tests together, to work.

When reusing a pattern, copy it fairly blindly first and then adapt it with refactoring or test-first, treating test-first, refactoring, and pattern-copying as elemental modes you switch rapidly between for focus without monotony.

Choose a system of development practices that support one another so you do about the right amount of each activity even under stress, designing virtuous cycles for good activities, avoiding death spirals, and adding negative feedback loops to prevent overuse.

Repair a misbehaving practice system by driving a positive loop the other direction (such as passing more tests to rebuild confidence), introducing a negative feedback loop to curb an overgrown activity, or breaking connections that form unhelpful loops.
Combine related assertions in a single test method when splitting them adds no communication value.
Generalize a literal by rewriting it as the expression it actually represents, then replacing the parts with the real computation.
